sermon:
## Blessed Before You Drew a Breath
*Every spiritual blessing, already yours, in Christ*

**Text:** Ephesians 1:1-14 · **Supporting:** John 15:16 · Romans 8:29-30 · 2 Corinthians 1:22 · Titus 3:5

Most of us live as if the Christian life were a transaction still being negotiated. We pray as people trying to secure something we are not sure we have. We obey as people trying to earn a verdict that has not come in yet. We wake up unsure whether God is for us this morning or merely tolerating us another day, waiting to see how we perform. And then Paul opens his mouth in the first chapter of Ephesians and says something so total, so finished, that it should end the negotiation before it starts. He does not begin with a problem. He begins with a blessing already given.

**He blessed us before we existed**
Paul does not begin with us at all. He begins with the Father. "Blessed be the God and Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, who has blessed us in Christ with every spiritual blessing in the heavenly places, even as he chose us in him before the foundation of the world, that we should be holy and blameless before him" (Ephesians 1:3-4). Read that slowly and notice the tense, because the tense is the gospel. He *has blessed*. Past. Complete. It is not a blessing being assembled as you improve; it is a vault already filled and already yours. And notice the timing of it — *before the foundation of the world*. Before the mountains were set. Before the first morning broke over the first sea. Before you had a name, or a wound, or a record of failures long enough to disqualify you ten times over. The choice was made in a love that predates everything you have ever done to deserve it and everything you have ever done to forfeit it. This is what unsettles the religious heart, because the religious heart wants the choosing to depend, even a little, on the chosen. Jesus closed that door himself, looking at men who thought they had found him: "You did not choose me, but I chose you" (John 15:16). We did not start this. We were chosen into it, by a Father who loved us before we were anyone at all.

**The Father chose, the Son redeemed, the Spirit sealed**
Watch the architecture of Paul's praise, because it is Trinitarian and it is deliberate, and once you see it you cannot unsee it. The Father chose us and predestined us for adoption "according to the purpose of his will, to the praise of his glorious grace" (Ephesians 1:5-6). The Son redeemed us: "In him we have redemption through his blood, the forgiveness of our trespasses, according to the riches of his grace" (Ephesians 1:7). And the Spirit seals us: "In him you also, when you heard the word of truth, the gospel of your salvation, and believed in him, were sealed with the promised Holy Spirit, who is the guarantee of our inheritance until we acquire possession of it" (Ephesians 1:13-14). Three Persons. One work. One people. This is the chain Paul lays out elsewhere with no link missing — "those whom he predestined he also called, and those whom he called he also justified, and those whom he justified he also glorified" (Romans 8:29-30). Not one of those whom he predestined is dropped before glory. And the Spirit is not a vague feeling of religious warmth; he is the legal deposit, the down payment God puts on you, "who put his seal on us and gave us his Spirit in our hearts as a guarantee" (2 Corinthians 1:22). A seal in the ancient world meant two things at once — ownership and protection. The seal said *this belongs to someone* and *this is not to be touched*. You are marked. You are kept. The transaction you keep trying to negotiate was closed by three divine Persons before you arrived in the room.

**Then stop pricing what is already paid**
Here is where it turns, and it turns onto us, because we say we believe all this and then live as the heirs of an estate who keep phoning the lawyer to ask whether the will is real. I have done it from inside this very calling. I have stood in a pulpit and preached free grace with everything in me, and then driven home and spent the week performing for God as if the sermon had been written for everyone but me, as if my standing still hung on whether I had a good week. We hear "every spiritual blessing" and the religious reflex fires instantly — we start an inventory of what we still lack, what we still need to secure, what we still have to become before the Father will look at us the way Paul says he already does. Paul will not allow the inventory. The grace is not measured according to our improvement; it is measured "according to the riches of his grace, which he lavished upon us" (Ephesians 1:7-8). Lavished. That is not the word for a careful, conditional, performance-based payout. And lest we imagine our salvation at least began with some better impulse in us, Scripture closes that escape too: he "saved us, not because of works done by us in righteousness, but according to his own mercy" (Titus 3:5). Now hear what Paul names three times in this single passage as the entire point of the whole thing — "to the praise of his glorious grace" (1:6), "to the praise of his glory" (1:12), "to the praise of his glory" (1:14). You were not chosen so that the universe would finally notice you. You were chosen so that the universe would finally see *him*. And this is the part no effort of yours can produce: every one of these blessings is held *in Christ*. The phrase falls again and again across these verses — in him, in Christ, in the Beloved. Not in your sincerity. Not in your track record. Not in your best Tuesday. In him. The Father has united all things in his Son and joined you to the Son, which means the blessing you keep trying to earn is locked in the One you could never earn. The church is his body precisely because she has nothing apart from her head, and needs nothing she does not already have in him.

Nothing was left for you to earn.

## The Prayer for Open Eyes
*Not new gifts, but sight to see the ones you have*

**Text:** Ephesians 1:15-23 · **Supporting:** 2 Kings 6:17 · Colossians 1:18 · Romans 8:11 · Philippians 3:8

If you were praying for a church you loved, a church you had bled for, what would you ask God to give them? Be honest. More members. More money. A break from the suffering. A door to open, a crisis to pass, a comfort to arrive. Now notice what Paul asks for, and notice as much what he does not. He has just spent fourteen verses telling this church that they already hold every spiritual blessing in Christ. And then he prays. And he does not pray for one more blessing on top of the pile. He prays that they would *see* the pile they are already standing on.

**Paul prays for sight, not supply**
"For this reason, because I have heard of your faith in the Lord Jesus and your love toward all the saints, I do not cease to give thanks for you, remembering you in my prayers, that the God of our Lord Jesus Christ, the Father of glory, may give you the Spirit of wisdom and of revelation in the knowledge of him, having the eyes of your hearts enlightened" (Ephesians 1:16-18). The eyes of your hearts. Paul understands something about us that we resist understanding about ourselves: our deepest problem is rarely lack. It is blindness to what we have already been given. We are not poor; we are sitting on a fortune in the dark. There is a moment in the sixth chapter of Second Kings that frames this whole prayer. Elisha's servant wakes at dawn to find the city ringed by an enemy army, horses and chariots everywhere, and he panics — and Elisha prays one short prayer over him: "O LORD, please open his eyes that he may see." And the LORD opened the young man's eyes, and he saw, and the hills were full of horses and chariots of fire all around Elisha (2 Kings 6:17). The fiery armies were already there. The servant simply could not see them, and so he was afraid of an enemy that was already outnumbered. That is exactly Paul's prayer for the church. Not *send the horses*. The horses are here. *Open the eyes.*

**Three things he wants them to see**
Paul does not leave the sight he prays for vague. He names three specific realities he wants the eyes of their hearts to behold: "that you may know what is the hope to which he has called you, what are the riches of his glorious inheritance in the saints, and what is the immeasurable greatness of his power toward us who believe" (Ephesians 1:18-19). Hope — a future already secured, not a wish. Inheritance — riches already deeded, not earnings still owed. Power — and here Paul refuses to let the word float as an abstraction, because we have heard the word *power* so often in religious talk that it has gone soft. So he measures it. How much power, exactly, is toward us who believe? "According to the working of his great might that he worked in Christ when he raised him from the dead and seated him at his right hand in the heavenly places" (Ephesians 1:19-20). That is the measure. Resurrection power. The precise force that broke open a sealed tomb and emptied it. And this is no distant historical event you read about; it is the live current running through you now, for the same Spirit "who raised Jesus from the dead dwells in you" (Romans 8:11). You are not waiting in line for that power to arrive someday. It is the power that has already raised you from spiritual death to spiritual life, and most of us walk around our whole lives unable to feel it under our feet.

**You already have what you cannot see**
Here is the turn, and it lands on us, on a people who own everything and live like beggars. We have been chosen, redeemed, sealed, and seated with Christ, and we crawl. We pray for what we already possess. We beg at the gate of a house we already own. I have done this with my whole heart and not known I was doing it — stood at the graveside of my own hope and pleaded with God to give me what he had already given me, because the grief had blinded me to it. The cure for that blindness is not more. More will not fix a sight problem. The cure is the prayer Paul prays — that the eyes of the heart would open and see what is already there. And he ends the prayer by lifting our eyes to the highest place there is, to where Christ sits at this moment. God "raised him from the dead and seated him at his right hand in the heavenly places, far above all rule and authority and power and dominion, and above every name that is named, not only in this age but also in the one to come. And he put all things under his feet and gave him as head over all things to the church, which is his body, the fullness of him who fills all in all" (Ephesians 1:20-23). Read where that power finally flows. He is the head. The church is the body. He is "the head of the body, the church... that in everything he might be preeminent" (Colossians 1:18). Which means the resurrection power that raised the head does not stop at the neck — it runs into every member of the body, into the hand that shakes, into the knee that buckles, into you. The same hand that emptied the tomb is the hand that holds you now. Paul counted everything else in his life as loss "because of the surpassing worth of knowing Christ Jesus" (Philippians 3:8) — not knowing *about* him, but knowing him, eyes open, seeing what was always there. That is the one thing worth praying for a church you would die for.

You already have what you cannot see.

## Dead, Then Alive
*Grace from the first breath to the last*

**Text:** Ephesians 2:1-10 · **Supporting:** Colossians 2:13 · John 5:25 · Romans 5:8 · Titus 3:5

We like to think of ourselves, before God found us, as sick. Wounded. Searching. Almost there, just needing a nudge. It is a flattering diagnosis, and we cling to it, because a sick man can still reach for the medicine, and a wounded man can still call for help, and a searcher is at least pointed in the right direction. It leaves us a little dignity, a little contribution, a little credit. Paul reaches for a harder word, and once you let it stand you cannot go back to the soft one. Not sick. Not wounded. Not searching. Dead.

**The diagnosis we will not accept**
"And you were dead in the trespasses and sins in which you once walked, following the course of this world, following the prince of the power of the air, the spirit that is now at work in the sons of disobedience" (Ephesians 2:1-2). Dead. Not falling behind, not struggling toward the light, not a fixer-upper with good bones. A corpse. And a corpse cannot improve itself, cannot reach for help, cannot cooperate with the paramedic, cannot meet the rescuer halfway across the room. It can only lie there. And Paul drives it further, into the very nature of the thing: "we all once lived in the passions of our flesh, carrying out the desires of the body and the mind, and were by nature children of wrath, like the rest of mankind" (Ephesians 2:3). By nature. This was not a rough season we were passing through. It was not a phase. It was what we *were*. And notice the pronoun in that verse, because Paul will not stand outside the diagnosis and point in. He does not say *you* were dead and *I* arrived to help the dying. He says *we all*. The man who would write half the New Testament filed himself under the same corpse-tag as the worst person you can picture. He is inside the body bag with the rest of us.

**The two words that change everything**
And then come two words on which the entire weight of the Bible turns, two words that should never be read without a held breath. "But God." "But God, being rich in mercy, because of the great love with which he loved us, even when we were dead in our trespasses, made us alive together with Christ — by grace you have been saved" (Ephesians 2:4-5). Read the timing, because the timing is where grace either is grace or is not. When did God make us alive? *Even when we were dead.* Not after we had cleaned ourselves up. Not once we showed some flicker of promise, some movement toward him he could reward. While we were still a corpse on the table, cold, contributing nothing. This is the gospel's stubborn and offensive order, the order it refuses to soften: "God shows his love for us in that while we were still sinners, Christ died for us" (Romans 5:8). The dead do not raise themselves and then get the credit. Jesus said it plainly: "the hour is coming, and is now here, when the dead will hear the voice of the Son of God, and those who hear will live" (John 5:25). You did not decide to live. You heard a voice in the dark of your death, and the voice was itself a resurrection, and you who could not move came up out of the grave. "And you, who were dead in your trespasses and the uncircumcision of your flesh, God made alive together with him, having forgiven us all our trespasses" (Colossians 2:13). All of them. Forgiven, before you knew their number.

**So there is nothing left to boast about**
Here is the turn, and Paul makes it for us before we can open our mouths to object, because he knows what we are. If you were dead and God made you alive, then you contributed to your salvation exactly what a corpse contributes to its own resurrection. Nothing. "For by grace you have been saved through faith. And this is not your own doing; it is the gift of God, not a result of works, so that no one may boast" (Ephesians 2:8-9). Read it slowly, because we are addicts of the boast — we will smuggle a boast into anything, even into our faith. Notice Paul closes that last exit too: even the faith is not the heroic act you mustered to impress him; the whole of it, faith and all, is the gift of God. He saved us "not because of works done by us in righteousness, but according to his own mercy" (Titus 3:5). And now, lest we hear all this and go limp, lest we decide that since works save nothing then works mean nothing, Paul springs the trap shut from the other side, in the very next breath: "For we are his workmanship, created in Christ Jesus for good works, which God prepared beforehand, that we should walk in them" (Ephesians 2:10). We are not saved by works. We are saved *for* them — for works he prepared before we drew breath, laid out ahead of us the way a path is laid before the one who will walk it ever arrives. Grace does not end our obedience; it is the only thing that births a real one. And every clause of this is *in Christ Jesus*. He is the resurrection life. We are his workmanship. The church is the body raised together with her head, and apart from the head she is still in the grave. The same God who stood over a formless dark and said *let there be light* stood over a dead man and said *let this one live* — and you stood up. That is not finally your testimony of how you found God. It is his testimony of how he found you, cold on the table, and called you by name.

Grace from first breath to last.

## The Wall Came Down
*Two peoples, one body, no wall*

**Text:** Ephesians 2:11-22 · **Supporting:** Galatians 3:28 · Colossians 1:20 · Isaiah 57:19 · John 17:21

Every human society draws a line and decides who stands inside it and who stands out. We are very good at this — it may be the thing we are best at. We draw the line by blood, by border, by accent, by income, by schooling, by the thousand small signals that tell us in a glance *this one is ours and that one is not*. The church in Ephesus had a line too, and not a petty one. It had the oldest and holiest line in the world — Jew and Gentile, the people of the covenant and everyone else, the circumcised and "the uncircumcision," a division God himself had once written into the law. And Paul says the cross walked straight up to that line, the holiest line on earth, and tore it down to the ground.

**Remember where you stood**
First Paul makes the Gentile believers remember, because grace only lands on people who have not forgotten they were strangers. "Therefore remember that at one time you Gentiles in the flesh... were at that time separated from Christ, alienated from the commonwealth of Israel and strangers to the covenants of promise, having no hope and without God in the world" (Ephesians 2:11-12). He refuses to let them romanticize their old position, refuses to let them imagine the outside was a fine and noble place to be. No hope. Without God. Strangers to the promise. Outside, in the cold, with nothing. That is the honest starting place, and we skip it at our peril, because a people who forget they were once outsiders very quickly start building walls of their own. "But now in Christ Jesus you who once were far off have been brought near by the blood of Christ" (Ephesians 2:13). Far off, brought near. Paul is reaching back and putting the prophet's own words in his mouth, the LORD's promise spoken centuries before: "Peace, peace, to the far and to the near, says the LORD" (Isaiah 57:19). The distance was real and it was vast. The blood closed it.

**The wall, and what tore it down**
Then Paul names the thing itself. "For he himself is our peace, who has made us both one and has broken down in his flesh the dividing wall of hostility" (Ephesians 2:14). His original readers would have seen it instantly, because in the temple in Jerusalem there stood an actual wall — a stone barrier separating the court of the Gentiles from the inner courts, with inscriptions posted on it warning that any Gentile who crossed the line did so on pain of death. That stone was the line made visible. Paul says Christ demolished it — and not by waving it politely away, not by declaring the old hostility a misunderstanding, but "in his flesh," in a body broken open on a cross, "by abolishing the law of commandments expressed in ordinances, that he might create in himself one new man in place of the two, so making peace, and might reconcile us both to God in one body through the cross, thereby killing the hostility" (Ephesians 2:15-16). Read where the hostility died. On the cross. Not at a negotiating table, not through a peace process, not by either side finally being reasonable. The very same blood that reconciled us to the Father reconciled us to one another, because "through him God was pleased to reconcile to himself all things, whether on earth or in heaven, making peace by the blood of his cross" (Colossians 1:20). You cannot be at peace with the Father and at war with his other children. The cross simply will not allow the arrangement. "There is neither Jew nor Greek, there is neither slave nor free, there is no male and female, for you are all one in Christ Jesus" (Galatians 3:28).

**Then stop rebuilding what he tore down**
Here is the turn, and it is uncomfortable, because we are wall-builders by nature and we are clever enough to baptize our walls and call them something holier. We separate by politics and name it conviction. We separate by class and name it preference. We separate by color and name it comfort or culture or just the way things are. And we do all of it *inside* the one body Christ died in his own flesh to make one. I have done it. I have stood in a pulpit preaching reconciliation to a room I had already quietly sorted in my own heart, already divided into the ones I was at ease with and the ones I tolerated. Paul will not have it from any of us. What Christ tore down with his own broken body, we have no business mortaring back together stone by stone, however good our reasons sound. And look at what he builds on the cleared ground where the wall used to stand: "So then you are no longer strangers and aliens, but you are fellow citizens with the saints and members of the household of God, built on the foundation of the apostles and prophets, Christ Jesus himself being the cornerstone, in whom the whole structure, being joined together, grows into a holy temple in the Lord. In him you also are being built together into a dwelling place for God by the Spirit" (Ephesians 2:19-22). Not two temples standing politely side by side. One. Christ the cornerstone that holds the whole thing square, the two ancient enemies set into the same walls, the Spirit of God moving through every room of the one house. This is the answer to the prayer Jesus prayed the night before the wall came down: "that they may all be one... so that the world may believe that you have sent me" (John 17:21). The unity of the church is not a program we run on a Sunday. It is a building he is building, and we are the stones, and not one of us belongs out in the cold any longer.

Two peoples, one body, no wall.

## The Mystery and the Power
*The church as God's wisdom on display*

**Text:** Ephesians 3:1-21 · **Supporting:** Colossians 1:26-27 · 1 Peter 1:12 · Romans 16:25-26 · John 17:23

We use the word mystery to mean a problem nobody has solved yet — a locked room, a missing clue, a puzzle waiting for the clever mind that will crack it. The Bible uses the word to mean almost the opposite. A mystery, in Paul's mouth, is a secret God kept hidden for ages and has now, in Christ, finally said out loud. Not a problem we must solve. A secret he has chosen to tell. Paul has been arrested and chained for preaching it, and in the third chapter of Ephesians he stops to tell us what the secret was — and then, having told us, he cannot stay on his feet about it. He gets on his knees.

**The secret hidden for ages**
"...how the mystery was made known to me by revelation, as I have written briefly. When you read this, you can perceive my insight into the mystery of Christ, which was not made known to the sons of men in other generations as it has now been revealed to his holy apostles and prophets by the Spirit" (Ephesians 3:3-5). And here, in the next line, is the content of the secret, the thing that lay hidden since before the foundation of the world: "This mystery is that the Gentiles are fellow heirs, members of the same body, and partakers of the promise in Christ Jesus through the gospel" (Ephesians 3:6). That is it. That is the secret the angels strained to glimpse. The mystery is not a hidden timeline or a coded prophecy or a key to the end of the world. It is a *people* — outsiders made heirs, strangers made family, the far-off seated at the same inheritance as the near, with no second-class seats. Paul says the same to the Colossians: "the mystery hidden for ages and generations but now revealed to his saints... which is Christ in you, the hope of glory" (Colossians 1:26-27). This is the thing into which "angels long to look" (1 Peter 1:12). The whole arc of redemption, kept under seal "for long ages" and now "disclosed and through the prophetic writings... made known to all nations" (Romans 16:25-26), breaks at last into the open — and what comes out into the light is a church made of every kind of person who had no earthly business being in the same room together.

**The church is the wisdom of God on display**
Now watch what Paul says this church is *for*, because it will reorder how you walk into a service on Sunday. "To me, though I am the very least of all the saints, this grace was given, to preach to the Gentiles the unsearchable riches of Christ... so that through the church the manifold wisdom of God might now be made known to the rulers and authorities in the heavenly places" (Ephesians 3:8-10). Through the church. Read it again. The display case God has chosen for his own wisdom is not the cosmos with its galaxies, not a cathedral with its stone, not even the preached sermon. It is the assembled people themselves — Jew and Gentile, the respectable and the wrecked, the executive and the addict, the lifelong member and the one who slipped in at the back this morning still unsure he belongs — seated together in one body. The watching powers of the unseen world look at *that*, at a reconciled people who could never have reconciled themselves, and they see a wisdom they could not have invented and cannot account for. The reconciled church is the sermon being preached to the heavens. You, sitting next to the person you would never have chosen, are the evidence. Jesus prayed it would work in precisely this way: "that they may become perfectly one, so that the world may know that you sent me and loved them even as you loved me" (John 17:23).

**So Paul bows, and we cannot grasp it standing up**
Here is the turn, and Paul makes it by falling to his knees, because some things cannot be grasped by a man standing up and reasoning at them. "For this reason I bow my knees before the Father, from whom every family in heaven and on earth is named, that according to the riches of his glory he may grant you to be strengthened with power through his Spirit in your inner being, so that Christ may dwell in your hearts through faith" (Ephesians 3:14-17). And then he prays for the one thing he knows full well lies beyond our reach unless God hands it over — "that you, being rooted and grounded in love, may have strength to comprehend with all the saints what is the breadth and length and height and depth, and to know the love of Christ that surpasses knowledge, that you may be filled with all the fullness of God" (Ephesians 3:17-19). Read that again and feel the paradox he leaves standing on purpose. He prays that we would *know* a love that *surpasses knowledge*. It will not fit inside our minds. It is too wide, too long, too high, too deep for the mind to close its hands around — and the only way Paul says we even begin to grasp it is "with all the saints." Together. In the body. Never alone, never as a private spiritual project. This is the self-implicating word for every one of us who has prized a solitary faith, who has imagined we could know Christ best off by ourselves: you cannot comprehend this love alone. It was always meant to be grasped in the company of the very people God reconciled to you, the ones in the next pew, the ones you did not choose. The mystery is the church, and the church is the room where the love is finally known. So Paul ends not with a tidy summary but with a doxology, because the only honest response to a thing this large is to praise it: "Now to him who is able to do far more abundantly than all that we ask or think, according to the power at work within us, to him be glory in the church and in Christ Jesus throughout all generations, forever and ever. Amen" (Ephesians 3:20-21). Glory in the church. The reconciled people are the very place his glory shows.

The church is God's wisdom on display.

## Walk Worthy, Grow Up
*Unity is kept, not built*

**Text:** Ephesians 4:1-16 · **Supporting:** Philippians 2:3 · 1 Corinthians 12:12 · Colossians 2:19 · John 13:35

The whole letter turns on the hinge of this chapter. For three chapters Paul has told us what God has done — chosen us, redeemed us, sealed us, raised us, reconciled us, made us one new people and a dwelling for his Spirit. He has been describing a gift. Now comes the word *therefore*, and everything that follows is the shape of a life that has actually understood the first half of the letter. "I therefore, a prisoner for the Lord, urge you to walk in a manner worthy of the calling to which you have been called" (Ephesians 4:1). Worthy. Not to earn the calling — that work is finished and was never ours to do — but to match it, to walk like people who are who Paul just said they are.

**The unity is already there; your job is to keep it**
And the first mark of a worthy walk is not the thing we would expect. It is not zeal, not boldness, not vision. It is humility. "With all humility and gentleness, with patience, bearing with one another in love, eager to maintain the unity of the Spirit in the bond of peace" (Ephesians 4:2-3). Read the verb carefully, because everything hangs on it. Not *create* the unity. Not *build* the unity. *Maintain* it. Paul does not command the church to manufacture oneness out of nothing, because the oneness already exists — the Spirit himself made it, and it is a fact before it is ever a feeling. "There is one body and one Spirit — just as you were called to the one hope that belongs to your call — one Lord, one faith, one baptism, one God and Father of all, who is over all and through all and in all" (Ephesians 4:4-6). Seven ones, hammered down in a row. The unity of the church is not a committee initiative or a vision-casting weekend. It is a settled fact about reality, accomplished by Christ, and our task is the humble, daily, unglamorous, unphotographable work of *not tearing it.* And that is exactly why the worthy walk has to begin with humility, because every single fracture in the body begins the same way — with someone, somewhere, quietly counting himself more significant than his brother. The cure is the mind of Christ, who taught us to "count others more significant than yourselves" (Philippians 2:3).

**Christ ascended and gave gifts to grow the body up**
Then Paul shows us where the gifts in the church come from, and it is not from the gifted. The ascended Christ — the one who descended into the low places and then "ascended far above all the heavens, that he might fill all things" (Ephesians 4:10) — "gave gifts to men" (Ephesians 4:8). "And he gave the apostles, the prophets, the evangelists, the shepherds and teachers" (Ephesians 4:11). Now notice the purpose Paul attaches to these gifted people, because it quietly dismantles every clergy-and-spectator arrangement the church has ever built and called normal. They are given "to equip the saints for the work of ministry, for building up the body of Christ" (Ephesians 4:12). Read it. The shepherd's job is not to do the ministry while the congregation watches and grades the performance. The shepherd's job is to equip the congregation to do the ministry themselves. The whole body works, or the body does not grow at all. "From whom the whole body, joined and held together by every joint with which it is equipped, when each part is working properly, makes the body grow so that it builds itself up in love" (Ephesians 4:16). One body, many parts, "and the parts do not all have the same function" (1 Corinthians 12:12) — and the growth of the whole thing comes down from the head and from nowhere else, "from whom the whole body, nourished and knit together through its joints and ligaments, grows with a growth that is from God" (Colossians 2:19). Cut a body part off from the head and it does not grow. It dies.

**So grow up, and stop being children**
Here is the turn, and it cuts close. Paul names the goal of all this gifting and equipping as maturity, plain and simple — "until we all attain to the unity of the faith and of the knowledge of the Son of God, to mature manhood, to the measure of the stature of the fullness of Christ" (Ephesians 4:13). And then he names the thing we are meant to grow out of, and it stings, because it describes so much of our church life: "so that we may no longer be children, tossed to and fro by the waves and carried about by every wind of doctrine, by human cunning, by craftiness in deceitful schemes" (Ephesians 4:14). Children. That is the diagnostic word for a church that knows all the songs but never matured past them, a church that is moved by whoever spoke last and loudest, that mistakes its preferences for convictions and its moods for the leading of the Spirit, that is blown sideways by every new wind because it never grew the weight to stand still. I have been that child, and I have led whole rooms full of them, and I have mistaken the noise of children for the health of the body. The cure is not more excitement, not another wave to ride. The cure is to grow up — "speaking the truth in love, we are to grow up in every way into him who is the head, into Christ" (Ephesians 4:15). The whole body grows in one direction only: up, toward the head, because the body's whole life is in the head, and a church is never one inch more mature than it is joined to Christ. And the watching world reads our maturity exactly the way Jesus said it would — not by our doctrine first, not by our buildings, but by the way the parts of the body love one another: "By this all people will know that you are my disciples, if you have love for one another" (John 13:35). The unity you keep is the sermon you preach to a world that builds nothing it cannot photograph.

Unity is kept, not built.

## Off With the Old, On With the New
*You are not who you were*

**Text:** Ephesians 4:17-5:21 · **Supporting:** Colossians 3:9-10 · Romans 13:14 · Romans 6:4 · 1 Thessalonians 5:5

There is a way of trying to change yourself that never works, and most of us have spent years and a great deal of strength on it. We try to behave our way into being someone new. We grit our teeth, we make the resolutions, we white-knuckle the old habit, and it holds for a while and then it doesn't, and we end up back where we started, more tired and more convinced we cannot change. Paul comes at the whole problem from the opposite end. He does not tell us to *become* new by force of effort. He tells us we already *are* new — and then says, given that, stop walking around in the clothes of the corpse you used to be.

**You were taught Christ; the old self is already dead clothing**
Paul reaches for the image of changing clothes, and he keeps it running through the whole passage. "You were taught... to put off your old self, which belongs to your former manner of life and is corrupt through deceitful desires, and to be renewed in the spirit of your minds, and to put on the new self, created after the likeness of God in true righteousness and holiness" (Ephesians 4:22-24). The old self is not the real you, straining heroically to get free. It is the grave-clothes — the wrappings of a man who is already dead. Paul says the same thing to the Colossians and puts it even more plainly in the past tense: "you have put off the old self with its practices and have put on the new self, which is being renewed in knowledge after the image of its creator" (Colossians 3:9-10). *Have* put off. *Have* put on. This is the engine underneath every single command that follows in this passage. Not white-knuckle self-improvement. Putting off what is already dead and putting on who you already are in Christ. "Put on the Lord Jesus Christ, and make no provision for the flesh, to gratify its desires" (Romans 13:14). You do not fight the old self into submission. You take it off, because it is dead, and you put on the new self, because it is alive, and it is you.

**So the new self walks differently — in truth, in love, in light**
And then Paul gets concrete, and he gets concrete fast, because the new self is not an inner glow; it is a man who lives differently on a Tuesday afternoon. "Therefore, having put away falsehood, let each one of you speak the truth with his neighbor, for we are members one of another" (Ephesians 4:25). "Let the thief no longer steal, but rather let him labor, doing honest work with his own hands, so that he may have something to share with anyone in need" (Ephesians 4:28). "Let no corrupting talk come out of your mouths, but only such as is good for building up, as fits the occasion, that it may give grace to those who hear" (Ephesians 4:29). "Let all bitterness and wrath and anger and clamor and slander be put away from you, along with all malice. Be kind to one another, tenderhearted, forgiving one another, as God in Christ forgave you" (Ephesians 4:31-32). Notice the standard underneath the forgiveness — *as God in Christ forgave you*. The cross sets the bar. And then the call rises higher still: "Therefore be imitators of God, as beloved children. And walk in love, as Christ loved us and gave himself up for us, a fragrant offering and sacrifice to God" (Ephesians 5:1-2). Walk in love — and the model of the love is a self given up, a cross. Then walk in light: "for at one time you were darkness, but now you are light in the Lord. Walk as children of light" (Ephesians 5:8). Read carefully what he says you are. Not that you are standing *in* the light, as if the light were merely around you. He says you *are* light, now, because you are joined to the One who is light — "for you are all children of light, children of the day. We are not of the night or of the darkness" (1 Thessalonians 5:5).

**Then stop living in clothes you already took off**
Here is the turn, and it lands squarely in the gap between what we are and how we still so often act. We have been raised with Christ, and we keep wandering back to the tomb to put the grave-clothes back on, because they are familiar and they fit the shape we held for so long. The bitterness we keep nursing because letting it go feels like losing. The lie we keep within easy reach because it is convenient. The cutting talk that tears another person down because, for one moment, tearing down feels like strength. These are not the new self struggling toward holiness. They are a dead man's wardrobe pulled back onto a living body, and when you say it out loud it sounds exactly as absurd as it is. I know that absurdity from the inside. I have stood up new in Christ on a Sunday and then spent the better part of a week back in the old coat, because the old coat asked nothing of me. Paul's final word here is not *try harder to be empty of the old.* It is *be filled with the new.* "And do not get drunk with wine, for that is debauchery, but be filled with the Spirit, addressing one another in psalms and hymns and spiritual songs, singing and making melody to the Lord with your heart, giving thanks always and for everything to God the Father in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ" (Ephesians 5:18-20). You do not drive out the old life by working harder at emptiness. You fill the new life so full of the Spirit that there is no room left for the old. And the whole of it flows from a death and a resurrection you were already joined to: "we were buried therefore with him by baptism into death, in order that, just as Christ was raised from the dead by the glory of the Father, we too might walk in newness of life" (Romans 6:4). The body that died with Christ rises to walk like Christ. The church puts on her own head, and she starts, slowly, to look like him.

You are not who you were.

## Christ and the Church at Home
*The gospel reaches the kitchen table*

**Text:** Ephesians 5:22-6:9 · **Supporting:** Colossians 3:18-4:1 · Philippians 2:5-8 · 1 Peter 3:7 · John 13:14

We are tempted to think the great truths of Ephesians live in the sanctuary, in the high air of doctrine, and that the kitchen table is where ordinary life takes back over and the theology gets put away with the good clothes. Paul thinks the exact opposite. He has spent five chapters on the largest things there are — eternal election, resurrection from the dead, the reconciled church, the cosmic powers in the heavenly places — and now he takes the entire weight of all of it and walks it straight through the front door of the house. Marriage. Children. Work. The places where no one is watching, where the cameras never reach, where a man is most truly himself. And he governs the whole household with one sentence that should hang carved over every door: "submitting to one another out of reverence for Christ" (Ephesians 5:21).

**The home is shaped by the marriage of Christ and his church**
Watch what Paul does with marriage, because it is not, at bottom, a list of household roles. It is a revelation of the gospel hidden inside a bedroom. "Wives, submit to your own husbands, as to the Lord" (Ephesians 5:22) — and then watch where the great weight of the passage falls, hard and long, not on the wife but on the husband: "Husbands, love your wives, as Christ loved the church and gave himself up for her" (Ephesians 5:25). Read where the standard is set. Not in authority, not in the right to be obeyed, not in a man's natural strength. The standard is the cross. The husband is not told to rule his wife; he is told to die for her, the way Christ died for his bride, "that he might sanctify her, having cleansed her by the washing of water with the word, so that he might present the church to himself in splendor, without spot or wrinkle or any such thing, that she might be holy and without blemish" (Ephesians 5:26-27). This is the mind of Christ poured into an ordinary marriage — the mind of the One who "emptied himself, by taking the form of a servant, being born in the likeness of men. And being found in human form, he humbled himself by becoming obedient to the point of death, even death on a cross" (Philippians 2:7-8). And then, lest we miss what this was always about, Paul tells us the secret beneath the whole institution: "This mystery is profound, and I am saying that it refers to Christ and the church" (Ephesians 5:32). Your marriage was never finally about you and the person you married. It is a small, lit theater in which the watching world is meant to see, in flesh and blood, how Christ loves his bride and how the bride answers her Lord.

**And it reaches the children and the workplace too**
Paul does not stop at the bedroom door. He keeps walking through the house, into the nursery and out to the workplace, and at every room he does the same thing — he turns and lays the harder word on the one holding the power. "Children, obey your parents in the Lord, for this is right" (Ephesians 6:1) — and immediately the turn onto the father: "Fathers, do not provoke your children to anger, but bring them up in the discipline and instruction of the Lord" (Ephesians 6:4). Then out into the world of work, where in Paul's day a master held the literal power of life and death over a bondservant: "Bondservants, obey your earthly masters with fear and trembling, with a sincere heart, as you would Christ... as servants of Christ, doing the will of God from the heart" (Ephesians 6:5-6), and once more the sharp turn onto the powerful — "Masters, do the same to them, and stop your threatening, knowing that he who is both their Master and yours is in heaven, and that there is no partiality with him" (Ephesians 6:9). The same Lord stands over the one with power and the one without, and he keeps no separate ledger for the important people. "For the wrongdoer will be paid back for the wrong he has done, and there is no partiality" (Colossians 3:25). The gospel walks into every uneven relationship in the house and tells the stronger party, in no uncertain terms, that he himself answers to a stronger Lord above him.

**So bring it home, where it actually costs**
Here is the turn, and it is the hardest preaching there is, because it is the most private. It is a comparatively easy thing to be a Christian in the pew on Sunday and a tyrant in the kitchen on Monday. We are experts at this. We reserve our best patience for strangers who will never see us again, and we spend our worst and rawest selves on the very people who share our name and our table and our last hour of every day. I have done it, and I will not pretend otherwise. I have preached self-giving love from a platform on a Sunday and then walked in my own front door that night too tired and too sour to give a single ounce of it to the five sons God entrusted to me. Paul will not allow the split. The same Christ who tore down the wall between Jew and Gentile reconciles husband and wife, parent and child, the powerful and the powerless, and he does all of it at the same cost — the cross. "If I then, your Lord and Teacher, have washed your feet, you also ought to wash one another's feet" (John 13:14). The husband is to live with his wife in an understanding way, "showing honor to the woman... since they are heirs with you of the grace of life" (1 Peter 3:7). None of this is technique, and none of it is a system for running a tidy household. It is the marriage of Christ and his church, lifted down off the wall of doctrine and set on the kitchen table where the dishes pile up and the children whine and the marriage is hardest to live — and where, precisely there, it is most clearly seen.

The gospel reaches the kitchen table.

## Standing in the Strength of the Lord
*Stand. The strength is his.*

**Text:** Ephesians 6:10-24 · **Supporting:** 2 Corinthians 10:4 · Isaiah 59:17 · Colossians 2:15 · Romans 8:37

We have read six chapters of pure grace, and now Paul ends the whole letter with a war. That is not a contradiction, and it is not a change of subject. It is the only honest way he could possibly end it, because a people this blessed will be opposed, and Paul refuses to send his beloved church out the door smiling and unarmed into a fight they did not know they were in. "Finally, be strong in the Lord and in the strength of his might" (Ephesians 6:10). Read the very first move of the command. Not *be strong.* Be strong *in the Lord*, in *his* might. The strength for this fight was never going to be yours, and Paul tells you so before he names a single weapon.

**Name the real enemy**
First Paul tells us what we are actually fighting, because we get this wrong almost every single time. "For we do not wrestle against flesh and blood, but against the rulers, against the authorities, against the cosmic powers over this present darkness, against the spiritual forces of evil in the heavenly places" (Ephesians 6:12). Not against flesh and blood. Read that again and let it land, because nearly every fight we actually pick is a fight with flesh and blood — the spouse across the table, the neighbor over the fence, the other political tribe, the person at church who wronged us, the relative who will not change. Paul says, with great care, that we have been misnaming the enemy this whole time. The human being standing in front of you is not the war. There is a darkness operating behind the visible, a real and unseen evil, and our weapons against *that* enemy cannot be the world's weapons — not our arguments, not our outrage, not our power plays, not our capacity to win and dominate. "For the weapons of our warfare are not of the flesh but have divine power to destroy strongholds" (2 Corinthians 10:4). And here is the trap underneath: the very moment you treat a fellow human being as your true enemy, you have already lost the real battle, and you have picked up the world's weapons to fight the wrong war.

**Put on armor that is not your own**
Then Paul hands us the armor, piece by piece, and the most striking thing about all of it is *whose* armor it actually is. "Put on the whole armor of God, that you may be able to stand against the schemes of the devil" (Ephesians 6:11). Every single piece — "the belt of truth... the breastplate of righteousness... as shoes for your feet, having put on the readiness given by the gospel of peace... the shield of faith, with which you can extinguish all the flaming darts of the evil one... the helmet of salvation, and the sword of the Spirit, which is the word of God" (Ephesians 6:14-17) — every one of these belongs first to God himself. Isaiah saw the LORD wearing this very armor centuries before Paul wrote a word of it: "He put on righteousness as a breastplate, and a helmet of salvation on his head" (Isaiah 59:17). The armor is God's own armor, taken off his own frame and buckled onto his soldiers. You do not bring your strength to this fight; you put on his. And notice the one verb Paul repeats like a drumbeat through the whole passage — four times he sounds it: *stand.* "Take up the whole armor of God, that you may be able to withstand in the evil day, and having done all, to stand firm" (Ephesians 6:13). The goal he sets is not to advance and conquer and seize new ground. The goal is to still be standing when the smoke finally clears. And the reason the goal is merely to stand is that the victory itself is already won — Christ, on the cross, "disarmed the rulers and authorities and put them to open shame, by triumphing over them in him" (Colossians 2:15). We do not fight in order to win. We stand in a win already accomplished by Another, on a hill, in a body, long ago.

**So stop fighting in your own strength**
Here is the turn, and it lands squarely on our self-reliance, which is the last and most respectable idol most of us surrender. We are a people who try to win our battles on our own steam, and then we sit exhausted and beaten and wonder why. We armor ourselves with our willpower, our cleverness, our hot outrage, our determination to handle it, and we march out, and we go down. I have done it more times than I would like to count — gone into the fight with my own strength carefully buckled on, certain I had enough, and come home defeated, because the strength was never mine to bring in the first place. And Paul's final weapon, the one he saves for last, is the one we are most likely to skip right past on our way to the fight: "praying at all times in the Spirit, with all prayer and supplication. To that end keep alert with all perseverance, making supplication for all the saints" (Ephesians 6:18). The fully armored soldier still kneels. And the prayer is not only for himself, off in his own foxhole — it is "for all the saints," because we stand together in this or we fall alone, and Paul, even from his chains, asks them to pray for him too (Ephesians 6:19-20). This is the church on her feet — the body wearing the armor of her own head, standing in his strength and not in hers, praying for one another in the smoke. And she does not lose, finally, because the One she is joined to has already triumphed and cannot lose. "No, in all these things we are more than conquerors through him who loved us" (Romans 8:37). Not by our strength. Through him who loved us. So stand — not because you are strong enough for the day, but because he is, and you are in him, and the war was won before you ever woke up to find yourself in it.

Stand. The strength is his.
